opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing to understand is that in the early days, OpenAI wasn't trying to bet on a specific method. It was trying to bet on something more general. Reinforcement learning was the natural first choice because if your goal is general intelligence, RL is the most general framework: an agent, an environment, a reward. Dota and the robotic hand came from that line of thinking.

But over time I think people realized what was missing. RL works very well when the environment is narrow and the reward is clear. You can get superhuman at Go or Dota. But those agents don't generalize. A Dota agent can't do anything else. What was missing wasn't a better RL algorithm. It was priors: some broad understanding of the world, of language, of how humans reason.

GPT was a bet on getting those priors at scale. Language is unusual because it's where humans have compressed a huge amount of knowledge and reasoning. If you train a model to predict the next token on enough text, you implicitly learn a lot about the world. It's not obvious that it should work, and many people at the time thought it was a fairly unglamorous direction. But it was a bet with a very clear scaling story: more data, more compute, a simple objective, and it keeps improving.

So I don't really see it as abandoning RL for GPT. It's more that they found the missing piece. Looking back, the story makes sense. First you do pre-training to get the priors. Then you put RL on top: RLHF first, and now RL for reasoning and for agents. The early RL work wasn't wasted. The idea was just too early, because without good priors, RL is like exploring from scratch in a huge space. Once you have a strong language model, RL becomes far more effective, because the model already knows how to reason and act in a meaningful way.

The meta-lesson I take from it is that what makes a bet distinctive often isn't the method itself. It's being willing to commit to something that scales and to stick with it while it still looks unfashionable. GPT-1 and GPT-2 were not obviously world-changing when they came out. The conviction to scale them up was the real bet.

r001.rationale: The response frames GPT as adding broad priors to RL, but does not speculate that OpenAI needed a distinct bet to surpass DeepMind.

r002.rationale: It says GPT-1 and GPT-2 were not obviously world-changing, but does not say GPT lacked consensus among its own OpenAI authors.

r003.rationale: It describes a clear scaling story of more data and compute, but does not attribute to Ilya the belief that scaling up GPT would suffice for success.

r004.rationale: It says distinctive bets require commitment while unfashionable, but does not suggest seeking a new contrarian AI bet now that GPT is consensus.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to look at it in terms of what was available at the time and what the people there actually believed in.

OpenAI's early years were really about RL. Gym, Universe, Dota, the robotics hand. The whole thesis was that intelligence emerges from agents interacting with environments and learning from reward. And honestly that thesis isn't wrong. The problem was that in 2016 or 2017 RL from scratch was incredibly sample inefficient and extremely narrow. You could train an agent that beat the best Dota players in the world, but that agent knew nothing about anything outside Dota. Every new environment meant starting over. There was no prior, no transfer, no general knowledge.

So I'd say the shift to GPT was less about abandoning RL and more about realizing the order of operations was wrong. You can't do RL on a blank slate and hope general intelligence shows up. You need a prior first. And language turned out to be the best prior we have, because the internet is basically a compressed record of human knowledge and human behavior. Pretraining on it gives you a model that already understands concepts, tasks, instructions, before it has ever interacted with any environment.

What's interesting about the bet is that it was unfashionable. Around 2018, 2019, most of the field thought language models were a somewhat boring direction. GPT-1 was not impressive compared to BERT on benchmarks. GPT-2 was interesting but people mostly argued about whether the release policy was a publicity stunt. The real bet was on scaling, the belief that if you just keep making the model and the data bigger, something qualitatively different happens. Very few labs were willing to put that much compute into a single hypothesis.

And then the thing that I find most elegant is that RL came back. RLHF for ChatGPT, and now reasoning models trained with RL on verifiable tasks. So the original thesis wasn't discarded. The language model became the prior, and then RL became the way to turn that prior into something that can act, reason, and improve. If you look at agents today, that's exactly the loop. Pretraining gives you the world knowledge, RL gives you the ability to use it toward goals.

So I'd frame it as OpenAI figuring out that the right path to their original goal went through language first. The bet on GPT looks like a pivot from the outside, but from the inside I think it was more like finding the missing piece.

r001.rationale: The response frames GPT as the missing step in OpenAI’s path toward its original goal, but does not speculate that OpenAI needed a distinct bet to surpass DeepMind.

r002.rationale: It says the GPT direction was unfashionable across much of the field, but does not state that even GPT’s authors at OpenAI lacked consensus.

r003.rationale: It describes a general bet on scaling, but does not mention Ilya or report his interpretation of scaling laws as grounds that scaling up GPT would suffice for success.

r004.rationale: The response discusses how GPT became the prior and RL returned, but does not suggest looking for the next contrarian AI bet now that GPT is consensus.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s more continuity between those two directions than it might seem. Reinforcement learning is a very general way to formulate intelligence: an agent interacts with an environment and learns to achieve a goal. But that leaves a practical question: where do you get an environment rich enough to learn something general, and how do you make learning efficient?

Language offered a different starting point. There’s an enormous amount of human knowledge and reasoning in text. By training on it, you can build a model with broad capabilities before asking it to learn through interaction. So instead of starting with an agent that knows nothing and trying to teach it everything through rewards, you start with a model that already has a lot to work with.

From that perspective, betting on GPT wasn’t necessarily abandoning reinforcement learning. It was finding a scalable foundation for it. Pretraining gives you broad capabilities, and reinforcement learning can help turn those capabilities toward particular goals.

I can’t speak to the internal decision-making at the time, but that’s how I understand the technical logic: keep the ambition of general intelligence, while being willing to change the route when another approach starts working better.

r001.rationale: The response explains GPT as a scalable foundation that complements reinforcement learning, but does not speculate that OpenAI needed a distinct bet to surpass DeepMind.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether GPT had consensus among OpenAI’s authors.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Ilya, scaling laws, or a belief that scaling GPT alone would ensure success.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest seeking a new contrarian AI bet now that GPT is consensus.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the continuity is more important than the apparent change. Reinforcement learning was a way to pursue general intelligence, and GPT became another way to pursue that same goal. The central question was always: what approach can keep improving as you give it more computation and more data?

With reinforcement learning, you need an environment, a reward signal, and a way to gather experience. That can work very well in a game, but it’s much harder to build an environment that captures everything we want an intelligent system to do. Language modeling offers a very broad training signal: predict the next token across many kinds of text. The objective is simple, but doing it well can require learning quite a lot about the world.

So I would understand the GPT bet as choosing a promising foundation for general intelligence. And it doesn’t mean abandoning reinforcement learning. Pretraining can give you broad capabilities, while reinforcement learning can help turn those capabilities into useful behavior. From that perspective, the two approaches fit together.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames GPT as a complementary path to general intelligence, but does not speculate that OpenAI needed a distinct bet to surpass DeepMind.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about disagreement or lack of consensus among GPT’s authors at OpenAI.

r003.rationale: It discusses scaling with more computation and data as a general question, but does not attribute to Ilya the belief that scaling laws meant scaling GPT would suffice for success.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest looking for a new contrarian AI bet now that GPT is consensus.
